Dobb takes the jug without a word, tips a long, glugging soak of oil down the gap, and hands you the first rag to light. You touch it to your lantern and drop it. The black throat answers with a soft *whump*, and an orange glow climbs the stones below. Smoke rolls up thick and bitter. You step back with your shield up, and the sound recedes into the dark.

Stone goes over it, and earth over the stone, and everyone stamps it down. After an hour and a quarter the corner is a solid, packed slope that looks as though it has been part of the bank for a century. A last test with the bar, shoved hard, doesn't move it.

At half past noon, nobody is hurt and the sun is still high. Marl lets out a whoop, and one of the Fenner cousins sits down on the heap and laughs, breathless. Dobb wipes his face and looks at you. "That'll hold a good while. Not for ever. They may find another way, or dig, if they're patient."

That was a real bit of work. The lower mouth is shut, the Lamp still burns, and the barn is full of people who will live. The ghouls are still in the barrow below, hungry and trapped between two lights. The upper mouth under the Lamp is Hob's to keep, and you promised to send word to him. You are out of prayers until tomorrow, with the afternoon ahead.

Maud does not move while you speak. Her hands stay flat on the chair back, and her knuckles go white, then slowly loosen. When you say he was not alone at the end, her mouth twists. When you take the shawl from your pack, she makes a small sound and puts the back of her wrist against her lips.

I take off my pack, set it on the table, and meet her eyes. "Yes, Maud. Hob died some time before the harvest feast, in the lamp-house, and nobody found him. I won't dress it up. But he did not leave the light, and he was not alone at the end: he kept it burning, and he saved a village by it."

I take out the blue shawl and hold it out in both hands. "He asked me to give you this. He said you wove it the winter he went up there, and I'm to tell you it was warm every night. He said to tell you he kept the light, that he wasn't afraid at the end." I add gently, "And he said you'd tell him he should have come home. He asked me to say he had somewhere to be."

input.add_to_description: Day 4 ~10 AM: received the shawl and Hob's words. Wept, laughed at "somewhere to be", then asked where he lies and whether he suffered. Brannoc has not yet told her Hob's remnant still keeps the Lamp. She wants to go up to the Lamp.

entries.text:
You set the pack on the table and say it plainly, the way you said it to the village: where he died, that no one found him, and that he did not leave the light. You hold the shawl out in both hands.

Maud does not take it at once. She looks at it as if it might bite. Then she lifts it and presses it to her face, and the faded blue wool muffles a sound that is half sob and half something else. Her shoulders shake. You stay where you are, and when the humming comes to you, you let it.

When you reach "he had somewhere to be", she laughs, one cracked, wet bark of a laugh, and sits down hard in the empty chair by the fire. "Somewhere to be. Forty years of other people's lamps, and he had somewhere to be." She wipes her face with the heel of her blue-stained hand. "That's him. That's exactly him. Stubborn old goat."

She is quiet for a time, the shawl in her lap, and the loom stands silent in the window. Then she looks up, and the sharp eyes are red but steady.

"Where is he? Not where he died, I know that. Where is he now? Is he buried? Did he go hard?" She grips the shawl. "I'll have the truth, young man. You said he saved a village. A lamp-keeper doesn't save a village by sitting still."

You know the truth is stranger than she imagines. Hob still sits on the lamp-house step with his unlit lantern. He spoke to you through a door, and he asked you to carry this message himself. She has asked you plainly, and what you say next will shape what she does.

How does Brannoc answer her?

sheet.opening: Brannoc Ashdown, a young human cleric of the Life domain, has been on the road only a few weeks, walking out from Millbrook Landing, the little river town of fishermen and reed-cutters where he grew up. He was orphaned at six when the Grey Fever emptied the houses along the water, and was raised by the temple's old healer, Mother Edda Thorne, who died last winter of old age and left him her plain wooden amulet. He keeps a promise to carry her work to places that have no healer at all. His past (true and not to be contradicted): as a child he sat beside dying neighbors because Edda had too few hands; the night she told him to leave a dying fisherman and rest, he refused, and the man's daughter later thanked him, which is the root of his stubbornness. He hums hymns while he works, is warm and patient, and swore never to let anyone suffer alone again. He is inflexible in his thinking. Open play on a muddy back road at dusk, at the edge of a small, struggling settlement with no priest or healer, its few lanterns lit early and its doors shut. Something has just happened that needs him: a frightened child or farmer hurries out to flag him down, begging for help for sick or wounded people sheltering in a barn, where the trouble is more than illness alone (for example, injuries from a recent attack by raiders or wild beasts, with the threat possibly still near). Brannoc has his mace, chain mail, shield, light crossbow, priest's pack, and 15 gp. Give him a clear, immediate call to act, and room to choose between healing, protecting, and investigating.
